questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: How many molecules of C$O_2$(g) are obtained on reaction of 24 grams of methane with 4moles of oxygen?
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the combustion of methane is:

$CH_4(g) + 2O_2(g) \rightarrow CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(l)$

Molar mass of $CH_4 = 16 \text{ g/mol}$

Moles of $CH_4 = \dfrac{24}{16} = 1.5 \text{ moles}$

Moles of $O_2$ given $= 4 \text{ moles}$

From the stoichiometry, $1 \text{ mole}$ of $CH_4$ requires $2 \text{ moles}$ of $O_2$. Thus, $1.5 \text{ moles}$ of $CH_4$ require $3 \text{ moles}$ of $O_2$. Since $4 \text{ moles}$ of $O_2$ are available, $CH_4$ is the limiting reagent.

Moles of $CO_2$ produced $=$ Moles of $CH_4$ reacted $= 1.5 \text{ moles}$

Number of molecules of $CO_2 = 1.5 \times N_A = 1.5 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 9.033 \times 10^{23}$

Answer: $9.033 \times 10^{23}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: 500 mL of an aqueous solution of glucose $C_6$H_{12}$O_6$ (Molar mass 180 gmol$^{-1}$) contains $6.02 \times 10^{22}$ molecules. The concentration of the solution will be:
questions.solution:
Number of moles of glucose is given by the ratio of the number of molecules to Avogadro's number.

$n = \dfrac{6.02 \times 10^{22}}{6.02 \times 10^{23}} = 0.1$ mol

Volume of the solution is $V = 500$ mL $= 0.5$ L.

Molarity is the number of moles of solute per liter of solution.

$M = \dfrac{n}{V} = \dfrac{0.1}{0.5} = 0.2$ M

Answer: $0.2$ M

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The mass of precipitate formed when 50 mL of 16.9% aqueous solution of $\text{AgNO}_3$ is mixed with 50 mL of 5.8% NaCl solution is------------g
[Ag = 107.8, N = 14, O = 16, Na = 23, Cl = 35.5]
questions.solution:
Mass of $\text{AgNO}_3$ in 50 mL of 16.9% solution = $\dfrac{16.9}{100} \times 50 = 8.45$ g

Molar mass of $\text{AgNO}_3$ = $107.8 + 14 + 3 \times 16 = 169.8$ g/mol

Moles of $\text{AgNO}_3$ = $\dfrac{8.45}{169.8} \approx 0.0497$ mol

Mass of NaCl in 50 mL of 5.8% solution = $\dfrac{5.8}{100} \times 50 = 2.9$ g

Molar mass of NaCl = $23 + 35.5 = 58.5$ g/mol

Moles of NaCl = $\dfrac{2.9}{58.5} \approx 0.0495$ mol

The balanced chemical equation is:

$\text{AgNO}_3 + \text{NaCl} \rightarrow \text{AgCl} + \text{NaNO}_3$

Since 1 mole of $\text{AgNO}_3$ reacts with 1 mole of NaCl, NaCl is the limiting reagent.

Moles of AgCl precipitate formed = $0.0495$ mol

Molar mass of AgCl = $107.8 + 35.5 = 143.3$ g/mol

Mass of AgCl formed = $0.0495 \times 143.3 \approx 7.1$ g

The closest integer value is 7 g.

Answer: $7$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: 20 g of $\mathrm{N}_2$ is made to react with 5 g of $\mathrm{H}_2$ to give ammonia. The limiting reagent and number of moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ formed respectively are:
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the formation of ammonia is: $\mathrm{N}_2(g) + 3\mathrm{H}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{NH}_3(g)$.

Calculate the initial moles of reactants:
Moles of $\mathrm{N}_2 = \dfrac{20 \text{ g}}{28 \text{ g/mol}} = 0.714 \text{ moles}$.
Moles of $\mathrm{H}_2 = \dfrac{5 \text{ g}}{2 \text{ g/mol}} = 2.5 \text{ moles}$.

Determine the limiting reagent:
According to the stoichiometry, 1 mole of $\mathrm{N}_2$ requires 3 moles of $\mathrm{H}_2$.
For 0.714 moles of $\mathrm{N}_2$, the required $\mathrm{H}_2 = 0.714 \times 3 = 2.142 \text{ moles}$.
Since the available $\mathrm{H}_2$ (2.5 moles) is greater than the required amount (2.142 moles), $\mathrm{N}_2$ is the limiting reagent.

Calculate the moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ formed:
From the stoichiometry, 1 mole of $\mathrm{N}_2$ produces 2 moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$.
Therefore, 0.714 moles of $\mathrm{N}_2$ will produce $0.714 \times 2 = 1.428 \text{ moles}$ of $\mathrm{NH}_3$.

Rounding to two decimal places, the moles of $\mathrm{NH}_3$ formed is 1.43 moles.

Answer: $\mathrm{N}_2$ and 1.43 moles

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: When one mole of a hydrocarbon $\mathrm{C}_{\mathrm{a}} \mathrm{H}_{\mathrm{b}}$ undergoes complete combustion, it requires 7.5 moles of $\mathrm{O}_2$ and results in the production of 6 moles of $\mathrm{CO}_2$. Calculate the values of $\mathrm{a}$ and $\mathrm{b}$.
questions.solution:
The combustion reaction of a hydrocarbon $C_{a}H_{b}$ is given by the equation:

$C_{a}H_{b} + (a + \dfrac{b}{4})O_{2} \rightarrow aCO_{2} + \dfrac{b}{2}H_{2}O$

Given that 6 moles of $CO_{2}$ are produced from 1 mole of hydrocarbon, we have $a = 6$.

Given that 7.5 moles of $O_{2}$ are required for complete combustion, we have the stoichiometric coefficient for oxygen:

$a + \dfrac{b}{4} = 7.5$

Substituting $a = 6$ into the equation:

$6 + \dfrac{b}{4} = 7.5$

$\dfrac{b}{4} = 7.5 - 6 = 1.5$

$b = 1.5 \times 4 = 6$

Therefore, $a = 6$ and $b = 6$.

Answer: $a=6$ and $b=6$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
If X is a haloalkane with a single Chlorine atom per molecule and the percentage of Cl is 55 , what would be the number of Cl atoms present in 0.1 g of the haloalkane?
Atomic mass of $\mathrm{Cl}=35.5 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$
questions.solution:
Let the molar mass of the haloalkane be $M$ g/mol. The percentage of Chlorine is given as $55\%$.

Since there is one Chlorine atom per molecule, the mass of Chlorine in one mole of the haloalkane is $35.5$ g. Therefore, $\dfrac{35.5}{M} \times 100 = 55$.

$M = \dfrac{35.5 \times 100}{55} = \dfrac{3550}{55} \approx 64.545$ g/mol.

The number of moles of the haloalkane in $0.1$ g is $n = \dfrac{0.1}{64.545} \approx 0.001549$ moles.

Since each molecule contains one Chlorine atom, the number of moles of Chlorine atoms is equal to the number of moles of the haloalkane, which is $0.001549$ moles.

The number of Chlorine atoms is $N = n \times N_{A} = 0.001549 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 9.328 \times 10^{20}$.

Answer: $9.328 \times 10^{20}$

questions.q:
An aqueous KCl solution of density $1.20 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mL}$ has a molality of $6.60 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{kg}$. The molarity of solution in $\mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{L}$ is .... (Nearest integer)
[Molar mass of $\mathrm{KCl}=74.5$]
questions.solution:
Given,
Density of KCl solution $=1.20 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mL}$
Molality of solution $=6.60 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{kg}$
Molar mass of $\mathrm{KCl}=74.5$
Molality $=\frac{6.60 \mathrm{~mol}}{\mathrm{~kg}}=\frac{6.60 \mathrm{~mol} \text { solute }}{1000 \mathrm{~g} \text { solvant }}$
$\begin{aligned} \\ \text { Mass of solution } & =6.6 \times 74.5+1000 \\ \\ & =1491.7 \mathrm{~g} \\ \end{aligned}$
$\text { Volume of solution }=\frac{\text { Mass }}{\text { Density }}=\frac{1491.7}{1.20}$
$\begin{aligned} \\ \text { So, molarity } & =\frac{6.60 \times 1.2}{1491.7} \times 1000 \\ \\ M & =5.3 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L} \\ \end{aligned}$
Nearest integer $=5 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$

$A_2(g)+3 B_2(g) \longrightarrow 2 A B_3(g)$
What is the total number of moles of the gases present in the container at the end of the reaction?
questions.solution:
Thus 1 mole of $A_2$ react with 3 mole of $B_2$
$\therefore 7$ moles of $B_2$ will react with $A_2=\frac{7}{3}$ moles
$A_2$ left $=5-\frac{7}{3}=\frac{8}{3}$ moles

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
When 1 mole of $\mathrm{O}_2$ and 1 mole of ammonia are made to react in the reaction,

$4 \mathrm{NH}_3(\mathrm{~g})+5 \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{NO}(\mathrm{g})+6 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(\mathrm{g})$
options: $1.0 \text { mole of NO will be produced }$
questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation is $4 \mathrm{NH}_3(g) + 5 \mathrm{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{NO}(g) + 6 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}(g)$.

Given initial moles are $n(\mathrm{NH}_3) = 1$ mole and $n(\mathrm{O}_2) = 1$ mole.

To find the limiting reagent, calculate the ratio of moles to stoichiometric coefficients:
For $\mathrm{NH}_3$: $\dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$
For $\mathrm{O}_2$: $\dfrac{1}{5} = 0.20$

Since $0.20 \lt 0.25$, $\mathrm{O}_2$ is the limiting reagent.

Using the stoichiometry of the reaction, 5 moles of $\mathrm{O}_2$ produce 4 moles of $\mathrm{NO}$ and 6 moles of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$.

Therefore, 1 mole of $\mathrm{O}_2$ produces:
$n(\mathrm{NO}) = \dfrac{4}{5} \times 1 = 0.8$ moles of $\mathrm{NO}$.
$n(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}) = \dfrac{6}{5} \times 1 = 1.2$ moles of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$.

Answer: $\text { Oxygen is the limiting reagent }$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What mass of Silver chloride, in grams, gets precipitated when $150 \mathrm{~ml}$ of $32 \%$ solution of Silver nitrate is reacted with $150 \mathrm{ml}$ of $11 \%$ Sodium chloride solution? Atomic mass in $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{mol}: \mathrm{Ag}=108, \mathrm{Na}=23, \mathrm{Cl}=35.5, \mathrm{~N}=14, \mathrm{O}=16$
questions.solution:
The chemical reaction is: $AgNO_{3} + NaCl \rightarrow AgCl + NaNO_{3}$.

Molar mass of $AgNO_{3} = 108 + 14 + 3 \times 16 = 170 \text{ g/mol}$.
Molar mass of $NaCl = 23 + 35.5 = 58.5 \text{ g/mol}$.
Molar mass of $AgCl = 108 + 35.5 = 143.5 \text{ g/mol}$.

Assuming the density of the solutions is approximately $1 \text{ g/ml}$, the mass of $150 \text{ ml}$ solution is $150 \text{ g}$.
Mass of $AgNO_{3} = 32\% \text{ of } 150 \text{ g} = 0.32 \times 150 = 48 \text{ g}$.
Moles of $AgNO_{3} = \dfrac{48}{170} \approx 0.2824 \text{ mol}$.

Mass of $NaCl = 11\% \text{ of } 150 \text{ g} = 0.11 \times 150 = 16.5 \text{ g}$.
Moles of $NaCl = \dfrac{16.5}{58.5} \approx 0.2821 \text{ mol}$.

Since the stoichiometry is $1:1$, $NaCl$ is the limiting reagent (as $0.2821 \lt 0.2824$).
Moles of $AgCl$ formed = Moles of $NaCl = 0.2821 \text{ mol}$.

Mass of $AgCl = 0.2821 \times 143.5 \approx 40.48 \text{ g}$.
Comparing with the given options, the closest value is $40.47 \text{ g}$.

Answer: 40.47

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A given mass of a hydrocarbon on complete combustion produced $176 \mathrm{~g}$ of $\mathrm{CO}_2$ and $90 \mathrm{~g}$ of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$. What is the Molecular formula of the compound?
questions.solution:
The combustion reaction of a hydrocarbon $C_xH_y$ is given by: $C_xH_y + (x + \dfrac{y}{4})O_2 \rightarrow xCO_2 + \dfrac{y}{2}H_2O$.

Calculate the moles of $CO_2$ produced: $n_{CO_2} = \dfrac{176 \text{ g}}{44 \text{ g/mol}} = 4 \text{ mol}$.

Calculate the moles of $H_2O$ produced: $n_{H_2O} = \dfrac{90 \text{ g}}{18 \text{ g/mol}} = 5 \text{ mol}$.

From the stoichiometry of the reaction, the moles of carbon atoms in the hydrocarbon equals the moles of $CO_2$, so $x = 4$.

The moles of hydrogen atoms in the hydrocarbon equals twice the moles of $H_2O$, so $y = 2 \times 5 = 10$.

The molecular formula of the hydrocarbon is $C_4H_{10}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{C}_4 \mathrm{H}_{10}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_2$ is used as an antacid. If a person, suffering from acidity, produces $2.5 \mathrm{~L}$ of Gastric juice in a day, approximately how many antacid tablets, each containing $600 \mathrm{~mg}$ of $\mathrm{Mg}(\mathrm{OH})_2$, will be required to completely neutralise the whole $\mathrm{HCl}$ produced in the stomach in one day? (Gastric juice contains $3.0 \mathrm{~g}$ of $\mathrm{HCl}$ per L). (Atomic masses: $\mathrm{Mg}=24 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}, \mathrm{O}=16 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$ & $\mathrm{H}=1 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$.)
questions.solution:
The total amount of $\mathrm{HCl}$ produced in the stomach per day is calculated as: Total $\mathrm{HCl} = 2.5 \text{ L} \times 3.0 \text{ g/L} = 7.5 \text{ g}$.

The molar mass of $\mathrm{HCl}$ is $1 + 35.5 = 36.5 \text{ g/mol}$. The number of moles of $\mathrm{HCl}$ is $n_{\mathrm{HCl}} = \dfrac{7.5}{36.5} \approx 0.2055 \text{ mol}$.

The neutralization reaction is: $\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2 + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgCl}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$.

From the stoichiometry, $1 \text{ mole of } \mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2$ neutralizes $2 \text{ moles of } \mathrm{HCl}$. Therefore, the required moles of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2$ is $n_{\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2} = \dfrac{0.2055}{2} = 0.10275 \text{ mol}$.

The molar mass of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2$ is $24 + 2(16 + 1) = 24 + 34 = 58 \text{ g/mol}$. The mass of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2$ required is $0.10275 \text{ mol} \times 58 \text{ g/mol} \approx 5.9595 \text{ g} = 5959.5 \text{ mg}$.

Each tablet contains $600 \text{ mg}$ of $\mathrm{Mg(OH)}_2$. The number of tablets required is $\dfrac{5959.5 \text{ mg}}{600 \text{ mg/tablet}} \approx 9.93$.

Rounding to the nearest whole number, $10$ tablets are required.

Answer: 10 tablets

questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the reaction between calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid is:

$\mathrm{CaCO}_{3} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaCl}_{2} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} + \mathrm{CO}_{2}$

The molar mass of $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ is $40 + 12 + 3 \times 16 = 100 \text{ g/mol}$.

The number of moles of $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ is $\dfrac{15 \text{ g}}{100 \text{ g/mol}} = 0.15 \text{ mol}$.

According to the stoichiometry of the reaction, $1 \text{ mole}$ of $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ reacts with $2 \text{ moles}$ of $\mathrm{HCl}$.

Therefore, $0.15 \text{ moles}$ of $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ will react with $0.15 \times 2 = 0.30 \text{ moles}$ of $\mathrm{HCl}$.

The molar mass of $\mathrm{HCl}$ is $1 + 35.5 = 36.5 \text{ g/mol}$.

The mass of $\mathrm{HCl}$ required is $0.30 \text{ mol} \times 36.5 \text{ g/mol} = 10.95 \text{ g}$.

Answer: 10.95 g of $\mathrm{HCl}$

questions.q: What would be the molarity of one litre solution of $22.2 \mathrm{~g}$ of $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$ ?
questions.solution:
The molar mass of $\text{CaCl}_{2}$ is calculated as follows:
Molar mass = $40.08 + 2 \times 35.45 = 40.08 + 70.9 = 110.98 \text{ g/mol}$.

Approximating the molar mass of $\text{CaCl}_{2}$ as $111 \text{ g/mol}$ for calculation:
Number of moles of $\text{CaCl}_{2} = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}} = \dfrac{22.2 \text{ g}}{111 \text{ g/mol}} = 0.2 \text{ mol}$.

Molarity ($M$) is defined as the number of moles of solute per litre of solution:
$M = \dfrac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{volume of solution in litres}} = \dfrac{0.2 \text{ mol}}{1 \text{ L}} = 0.2 \text{ M}$.

Answer: $0.2 \mathrm{M}$

$60 \mathrm{~g}$ of acetic acid requires $=46 \mathrm{~g}$ of ethyl alcohol $20 \mathrm{~g}$ of acetic acid requires $=\frac{46}{60} \times 20=15.3 \mathrm{~g}$ of ethyl alcohol
Therefore, ethyl alcohol is the limiting reagent.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The mass of oxygen gas which occupies $5.6 \mathrm{~L}$ at STP would be
options: the gram atomic mass of oxygen
one-fourth of the gram atomic mass of oxygen
double the gram atomic mass of oxygen
half of the gram atomic mass of oxygen
questions.solution:
Mass of oxygen in $22.4 \mathrm{~L}$ at STP $=32 \mathrm{~g}$
Mass of oxygen in $5.6 \mathrm{~L}$ at $\mathrm{STP}=\frac{32}{22.4} \times 5.6=8 \mathrm{~g}=\frac{1}{2} \times$ gram atomic mass of oxygen
Therefore, mass of oxygen gas in 5.6 L at STP would be the half of the gram atomic mass of oxygen.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Density of $3 \mathrm{M}$ solution of $\mathrm{NaCl}$ is $1.25 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mL}$. The mass of the solvent in the solution is
questions.solution:
\begin{aligned}
&\text d=1.25 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mL} \text {, conc. of solution }=3 \mathrm{M}\\
&=3 \text { moles in one litre of the solution. }\\
&\text { Molar mass of } \mathrm{NaCl}=23+35.5=58.5 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}\\
&\text { Volume of solution }=1 \mathrm{~L}=1000 \mathrm{~mL}\\
&\text { Mass of solution }=d \times V\\
&=1.25 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mL}^{-1} \times 1000 \mathrm{~mL}=1250 \mathrm{~g}\\
&\text { Mass of solute }(\mathrm{NaCl})=n \times \text { molar mass }\\
&=3 \times 58.5=175.5 \mathrm{~g}\\
&\text { Mass of solvent }=\text { mass of solution - mass of solute }\\
&=1250-175.5=1074.5 \mathrm{~g}
\end{aligned}

questions.q: The mole fraction of benzene in a solution containing $39 \%$ by mass in an organic solvent of molecular mass 122 is
questions.solution:
Given, $39 \%$ by mass of organic solvent in benzene $\therefore 39 \mathrm{~g}$ of organic solvent in $100 \mathrm{~g}$ solution.
or
$39 \mathrm{~g}$ of organic solvent in $100-39=61$ g benzene.
Now, molar mass of organic solvent $=122 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$
Molar mass of benzene $\left(\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{6}\right)=12 \times 6+6=78 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}\therefore$ Moles of benzene $\left(n_{B}\right)=\frac{61}{78}$
Moles of organic solvent $\left(n_{\mathrm{O}}\right)=\frac{39}{122}$
Mole fraction of benzene $=\frac{n_{B}}{n_{B}+n_{\mathrm{O}}}=\frac{\frac{61}{78}}{\frac{61}{78}+\frac{39}{122}}=0.6$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The mass of hydrogen in gram required to completely saturate 1 mole of triolein is
questions.solution:
One mole of triolein contain three double bonds. Hence, during hydrogenation, it adds three moles of hydrogen.
One mole of hydrogen $=2 g$.
$\therefore$ Three moles of hydrogen $=6 \mathrm{~g}$.
